# Mucalinda Sutta (Ud 2.1 (PTS Ud 10))

**ID:** Ud 2.1 (PTS Ud 10)
**Section:** Udāna (ud)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-2
**Title (Pali):** Mucalinda Sutta
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ud2.1
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0503m.mul1.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mucalinda Sutta* (Ud 2.1; PTS Ud 10) is the opening discourse of the second chapter (*Mucalindavagga*) of the *Udāna* [SuttaCentral; Anandajoti 2010]. Set shortly after the Buddha's awakening under the Mucalinda tree near Uruvelā, the narrative relates that a severe, unseasonable storm arose [SuttaCentral; Anandajoti 2010; Buswell & Lopez 2014]. In response, the serpent king (*nāgarājā*) Mucalinda emerged from his subterranean abode, wrapped his coils seven times around the Buddha's body, and spread his broad hood overhead like a canopy to protect him from the cold, heat, wind, and biting insects [Anandajoti 2010; Buswell & Lopez 2014]. When the sky cleared, Mucalinda uncoiled, assumed the guise of a young youth, and paid homage, prompting the Buddha to utter an inspired verse (*udāna*) celebrating the happiness of seclusion, peaceful contentment, and freedom from craving [Anandajoti 2010]. This famous episode became one of the most prominent iconic themes in Buddhist art and narrative tradition [Sujato 2012; Buswell & Lopez 2014].

The sutta shares substantial textual and narrative material across early Buddhist literature. SuttaCentral identifies passage-level parallels in the Theravāda *Vinaya* (*Mahākhandhaka*, Kd 1), the Sanskrit *Saṅghabhedavastu* (Kd 17), the *Udānavarga* (UV 30, *Sukhavarga*), two Chinese translations of the *Udāna* (T 212.31 and T 213.30), and the Tibetan *Udānavarga* (Uv Kg 30), along with cross-references in the *Kathāvatthu* (Kv 2.8) and *Peṭakopadesa* (Pe 2) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus strongly corroborates these connections: its Pali text-reuse alignments show that the bulk of the *Mucalinda Sutta* (§1.3–6.4) is virtually identical to the *Mahākhandhaka* narrative (Kd 1, §3.1.1–3.4.8), shares identical verse segments with the *Kathāvatthu* (Kv 2.8, §4.1–6.4), and shares opening stock phrasing with the *Bodhi Suttas* (Ud 1.1–1.3) [DharmaNexus; Anandajoti 2010]. Across languages, DharmaNexus automatically aligns the text with Sanskrit biographical cycles in the *Saṅghabhedavastu*, the *Catuṣpariṣatsūtra*, and the *Lalitavistara*, as well as the Tibetan *Abhiniṣkramaṇa-sūtra* (D0301) [DharmaNexus], confirming the widespread transmission of the Mucalinda narrative across northern and southern Buddhist textual traditions [Allon, The Senior Manuscripts; Nakamura, Gotama Buddha].
